content: Young adult albino rats, with an average weight of 165 grams, were divided into five groups, each consisting of five males and five females, for studies involving tributyltin fluoride (TnBTF). No control group was described in these studies. The animals were exposed to TnBTF in a test chamber for four hours, during which mortality and behavioral reactions were recorded. After exposure, the animals were observed for an additional period. Autopsy findings in some animals revealed mild to severe focal discoloration of the lungs and lung enlargement. The acute inhalation toxicity of dimethyltin dichloride (DMDC) vapor was evaluated in the presence of varying amounts of trimethyltin chloride (TMTC) contaminant. Young adult Charles River albino rats, grouped into five males and five females, were exposed to DMDC for one hour. Mortality and behavioral reactions were monitored for 21 days. Nominal vapor concentrations were calculated based on the weight loss of the test material and the total volume of air used. At the end of the 21-day observation period, the animals were euthanized, and gross pathological examinations were conducted. At a concentration of 87% TMTC (1,428 mg/m³ as tin), no deaths occurred. Body weight gains were normal, and autopsy revealed no gross pathological alterations. At 0.09% TMTC (1,142 mg/m³ as tin), all animals died within 11 days, exhibiting hypoactivity, roughened fur, ptosis, enophthalmos, anesthesia, and tremors. However, autopsy findings showed no abnormalities attributable to DMDC toxicity. At 59% TMTC (2,205 mg/m³ as tin), similar results were observed, except all animals died within four days. At 0 mg/m³ as tin, animals displayed roughened fur, hypoactivity, ptosis, and salivation during the 14-day observation period, but no deaths occurred. Body weight gains were normal, and autopsy revealed no gross pathological alterations. All rats exposed to TMTC at a concentration of 8,890 mg/m³ (5,334 mg/m³ as tin) died on the first day. Observed signs included hypoactivity, roughened fur, enophthalmos, ptosis, anesthesia, and dyspnea. Autopsy findings revealed no abnormalities attributable to TMTC. Two vapor inhalation studies were conducted to determine the toxic effects of tributyltin chloride (TBTC) and tributyltin bromide (TBTB) on rats. Microscopic examinations of the brain, lungs, liver, and kidneys were performed. The only significant difference from controls was observed in liver weight, which was higher than control values after two months of exposure and lower one month after the end of exposure. Microscopically, the liver showed phagocytizing Kupffer cells that were swollen and proliferating, small areas of necrosis, moderate fibrotic expansion of the periportal areas, and fine to medium droplets of fatty degeneration. Liver damage increased in severity with the length of exposure and was not reversed after exposure ceased. Four months after exposure, the kidneys exhibited interstitial proliferation of inflammatory cells and an accumulation of cell debris and eosinophils in the tubules. The brain showed massive arterial hyperemia, pronounced cerebral edema, and cellular necrosis. Brains examined one month after the end of exposure showed signs of returning to normal. These results indicated that severe brain damage caused by TBTC might be asymptomatic. Iwamoto conducted a series of inhalation experiments to study the effects of TBTB on the reproductive functions of rats. Mature male and female rats, weighing 200–320 grams and 150–180 grams, respectively, were exposed to TBTB in a test chamber maintained at approximately 20°C at a concentration of 2 mg/m³, measured as tin, using a quartz spectrophotometer. The concentration of TBTB in the chamber was maintained by aeration of a TBTB mixture kept in the chamber. Five females exposed for five hours per day for 38 days and mated to unexposed males during non-exposure hours in the last 28 days had a pregnancy rate of 60%, compared to 100% in controls. Ten females exposed for five hours per day for six weeks, with mating occurring during non-exposure hours for the last four weeks, had a pregnancy rate of 10%. Partial recovery of reproductive capabilities in the exposed rats occurred within 16 days after exposure ended. Three groups of five females exposed for two hours per day for two, three, or four months, with mating occurring during the last four weeks, had pregnancy rates of 60%, 20%, and 0%, respectively. Partial recovery of reproductive capabilities was observed one week after exposure ended in all females exposed for three months and 10 days after exposure ended in all females exposed for four months. Two groups of five males exposed for five hours per day for two or seven weeks, followed by a five-hour-per-day exposure during a four-week mating period, impregnated all unexposed females. When five males and five females were exposed for five hours per day for six weeks, with mating during the last four weeks, no pregnancies occurred. Microscopic examination of the sex organs of three males exposed for 79–80 days, three females exposed for 42 days, four females exposed for 42 days and allowed to recover for 7–28 days, five females exposed for 7–14 days, and ten females exposed for 14 days with a 7–28-day recovery period revealed no effects on the male sex organs.
